row.label: Consult PostgreSQL’s transaction-isolation

selected_quotes: One important aspect of transactions in PostgreSQL, and therefore in all other modern relational databases, is the ability to control when a row is visible to a user and when it is not.
The two most commonly used transaction isolation levels are READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ.

row.label: continuous-archiving documentation. Contrast snapshot timing under Read Committed

selected_quotes: In READ COMMITTED mode, every SQL statement will see changes which have already been committed (e.g. new rows added to the database) by some other transactions.
However, within a statement the data you see is constant – it does not change.
A SELECT statement (or any other statement) will not see changes committed WHILE the statement is running.
Within an SQL statement, data and time are basically “frozen”.

In the case of REPEATABLE READ the situation is quite different: A transaction running in REPEATABLE READ mode will never see the effects of transactions committing concurrently – it will keep seeing the same data and offer you a consistent snapshot throughout the entire transaction.
If your goal is to do reporting or if you are running some kind of data warehousing workload, REPEATABLE READ is exactly what you need, because it provides consistency.
All pages of your report will see exactly the same set of data.
There is no need to worry about concurrent transactions.
